name: Femi Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy drinks for Castlegate Drinks, a distributor that supplies corner shops, pubs and takeaways around the city's east side. Soft drinks, bottled water, energy drinks, some beer. Every morning I check the weather and the fixtures list, because a heatwave or a big football match changes everything, and I've got an AI setup that turns that into suggested orders. I like being right about a hot weekend. What drains me is suppliers putting prices up with a week's notice.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my younger brother Tunde, who's at college, and I send a bit home to my mum every month. So even though I earn all right on paper, at the low end for buyers really, I've got under a month saved. On Sundays it's church and then my uncle's for lunch. And I've got a plan to import West African malt drinks and ginger beer for the local shops one day, on my own account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good, but there's no magic, you still need to work hard. At work I'd keep showing people my setup. Online I'd probably post something about how the winners are the ones who use tools and still graft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'm betting on these tools to give me an edge. But my job would be safe, and that's not nothing with my mum relying on me. The real issue is I don't earn enough to save for my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep improving my order predictions. I'd start the import idea small, one pallet of malt drinks sold to ten shops I know, about six hundred to start. And I'd try to save something every month even with the money to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I'd want things to move faster for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the six hundred for that first pallet come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months of no takeaways and no new trainers, plus some overtime in the summer. I wouldn't borrow for it. My uncle says never start a business owing money, and he's run his shop for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Castlegate mind you selling on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mr Okafor, the owner, up front, because it's not competition, it's a line Castlegate doesn't carry. If he wanted it, I'd even sell it through them. Honesty with your boss is cheaper than getting caught.

I'd post that winners **use tools** and still work hard.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I'm betting on AI for an edge.
My real issue is not earning enough to save for **my own business**.
do: Keep improving his **order predictions** at work.
Start the import idea with **one pallet** of malt drinks, about six hundred.
Save **something monthly** despite sending money to his mum.
feel: **Fine** but impatient for things to move faster.
S0.quote: My uncle says never start a business owing money, and he's run his shop for twenty years.
fieldNote: His plateau worry is **slow progress**, not losing the job.
Money he sends to his **mum** keeps his savings near zero.
He plans a **side business** carefully, with no borrowing.

steps.text: Keep refining his weather and fixtures order predictions
Sell one pallet of malt drinks to ten local shops
Skip takeaways for two months to fund the first pallet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be someone who already uses the tools. At work I'd offer to roll out the system for the whole buying team. Online I'd tell people to learn it now rather than complain later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the ones who stays, because I already do half of it with AI. Castlegate goes from four buyers to two, and I'd bet on me being one. But I'd also see the writing on the wall and speed up my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build out the automated ordering for the whole team within six months and make myself the person who runs it. I'd use the time I save to grow the import line, maybe three pallets a month. And I'd spend about a thousand on a small storage unit near the ring road for stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit guilty about the colleagues who'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Gloria has been buying beer for fifteen years and still uses paper, and I'd try to get her moved to the customer side. She'd be talking to pub landlords, where she's brilliant. She's kind and she taught me a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A thousand on a storage unit is more than you've got saved. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd do it in stages, start with a corner of my uncle's shop storeroom and only rent the unit once sales cover it. I get excited and have to slow myself down.

Store stock in his **uncle's storeroom** before renting a unit.

fieldNote: He expects to be **kept** because he already works with AI.

He'd look out for a **paper-based colleague** who taught him.

steps.text: Build automated ordering for Castlegate's whole buying team
Grow the malt drinks import line to three pallets a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit hard, and people need to help themselves and each other, not just wait. At church I'd say we should organise, help people find work. At work I'd say let's be honest about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even I'm out by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it doesn't need me to run it. And my import idea gets harder too, because big firms will run their buying with AI and undercut me. The one thing robots can't do until 2031 is carry crates, so the hands-on side lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Castlegate as long as they'd pay me and save hard. I'd buy a second-hand van for about four thousand on a small loan, against my uncle's advice, and deliver my own drinks plus other people's. Delivering and stacking shelves gives me the three years before robots. And Tunde and I would cut to the bone so Mum still gets her money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I've always had a plan, and this one cuts it short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go against your uncle's advice. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because two years doesn't leave time to save four thousand on my pay. It's a risk either way. My uncle would be disappointed, but he'd understand. He came here with one suitcase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and the money will keep coming. Then I'd make it true somehow. As the eldest son, I wouldn't let my mum worry, even if that means extra shifts at my uncle's shop.

say: I'd say people must **help themselves** and each other, not just wait.
I'd suggest at church we **organise** to help people find work.
think: Even I'm **out by 2028**, since AGI doesn't need me to run it.
Big firms with AI would **undercut** my import idea.
do: Stay at Castlegate as long as possible and **save hard**.
Buy a second-hand **van** for about four thousand to deliver drinks.

feel: **Alarmed**, because his plan gets cut short.
S2.quote: As the eldest son, I wouldn't let my mum worry, even if that means extra shifts at my uncle's shop.
fieldNote: Even the most **adaptive** buyer expects to be out by 2028.
He'd move to **hands-on** delivery to buy three years before robots.
Duty to his **mother** shapes every money decision.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand van to deliver drinks to local shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work at it. At church I'd talk to the young men about trades and small businesses. At work I'd keep pushing the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me maybe three more years at Castlegate and time to build the import line properly. I'd want it big enough to support me by 2030. The thinking side of my business, ordering and pricing, gets cheaper with AI, which actually helps a small firm like mine. The van and the lifting last until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate as much of my own import business as I can now: orders, invoices, stock. I'd save four thousand over two years for a van, no loan. And I'd grow to twenty shops before I leave Castlegate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but fired up. It's a race, and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does AGI help or hurt your business idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The paperwork side becomes almost free, so I can run a firm alone. But every other small importer gets the same tools. A machine doesn't have an uncle in the community, and that trust from shop owners is what my business has got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still send money home in these years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always. Maybe less for a year while I save for the van, and I'd explain why to Mum. She'd say build the business first. She's tougher than me.

I'd talk at church about **trades and small businesses**.

Cheaper **AI paperwork** actually helps a one-man firm like mine.

Save **four thousand** over two years for a van, no loan.
Grow to **twenty shops** before leaving Castlegate.
feel: **Nervous but fired up**, enjoying the race.

fieldNote: He sees AGI making **paperwork** cheap enough for a one-man firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance for anyone who wants to build something. At work I'd say use the tools and get ahead. Online I'd encourage people to start small businesses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for me. I'd likely stay a buyer for a few years, then go full-time on my own business by about thirty-two. By 2036 I'd want staff of my own, maybe two drivers, and to own the van and a small unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing automation at Castlegate and save hard for three years. Then I'd buy a van and rent a small unit. I'd use AI for all my business paperwork from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Money's tight, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want staff of your own. Would you use robots instead, when they come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually, in 2039. But I'd want to give my brother and cousins jobs first. A business should help your family stand up, not just make the owner money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm thirty-seven and still haven't saved for a house because I put everything into the business. My uncle says that's normal. My mum says find a wife first.

I'd encourage people online to **start small businesses** now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it cuts my plan short before I've saved anything. What would help is cheap start-up loans for small businesses, not handouts. And rules that stop the giant firms from crushing every small supplier on price.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. Everything I'd do, I'd do for my mum and my brother. People talk about jobs like it's just one person, but my job feeds three.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: People talk about jobs like it's just one person, but my job feeds three.
portrait: Femi is a 27-year-old **drinks buyer** for a city distributor who uses AI daily for weather-based orders.
He shares a flat with his brother and sends money to his **mum**, so he has under a month saved.
He dreams of importing **West African drinks** and plans it carefully, with his uncle's no-debt advice.
He sees opportunity in **slower scenarios** but expects even himself to be out by 2028.
His values are **family, church and work**, and he wants loans, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, cutting short his business plan before he's saved.
whatWouldHelp: Rules stopping **giant firms** from crushing small suppliers on price.
